etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English pyne, from Latin pīnus, from Proto-Indo-European *peyH- (“sap, juice”). Cognate with Sanskrit पितु (pitu, “sap, juice, resin”). Doublet of pinus. Related to fat.

definitions.definition: (countable, uncountable) Any coniferous tree of the genus Pinus.

quote.citation: 1913, Joseph C[rosby] Lincoln, chapter I, in Mr. Pratt’s Patients, New York, N.Y., London: D[aniel] Appleton and Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: I stumbled along through the young pines and huckleberry bushes. Pretty soon I struck into a sort of path that, I cal'lated, might lead to the road I was hunting for. It twisted and turned, and, the first thing I knew, made a sudden bend around a bunch of bayberry scrub and opened out into a big clear space like a lawn.

quote.citation: 1963, Margery Allingham, “Miss Thyrza’s Chair”, in The China Governess: A Mystery, London: Chatto & Windus, →OCLC, page 41:
quote.text: Sepia Delft tiles surrounded the fireplace, their crudely drawn Biblical scenes in faded cyclamen blending with the pinkish pine, while above them, instead of a mantelshelf, there was an archway high enough to form a balcony with slender balusters and a tapestry-hung wall behind.

definitions.definition: (countable) Any tree (usually coniferous) which resembles a member of this genus in some respect.
(archaic except Caribbean, Guyana, South Africa, Australia) A pineapple.

quote.citation: 1847 January – 1848 July, William Makepeace Thackeray, Vanity Fair […], London: Bradbury and Evans […], published 1848, →OCLC:
quote.text: " […]  I bought a pine-apple at the same time, which I gave to Sambo. Let's have it for tiffin; very cool and nice this hot weather." Rebecca said she had never tasted a pine, and longed beyond everything to taste one.

quote.citation: 1918 June, Katherine Mansfield [pseudonym; Kathleen Mansfield Murry], “Prelude”, in Bliss and Other Stories, London: Constable & Company, published 1920, →OCLC, chapter 7, pages 38–39:
quote.text: Linda carried the oysters in one hand and the pineapple in the other.  […]  [S]he put the bottle of oysters and the pine on a little carved chair.

definitions.definition: (sports, uncountable, colloquial) The bench, where players sit when not playing.

quote.citation: 2013, Sam Zygner, The Forgotten Marlins, page 287:
quote.text: […]  rather than languish on the pine in Miami.

quote.citation: 2019, Martin Copeland, The Boys from Dogtown:
quote.text: Take off your gear and hit the pine. And don't take your time. You understand me, boy?

etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English pine, pyne, from Old English *pīn (“pain”), from Proto-Germanic *pīnō (“pain, torment, torture”), possibly from Latin poena (“punishment”), from Ancient Greek ποινή (poinḗ, “penalty, fine, bloodmoney”). Cognate to pain.

Entered Germanic with Christianity; cognate to Middle Dutch pinen, Old High German pīnōn, Old Norse pína.

From Middle English pinen, from Old English pīnian (“to torment”), from Proto-Germanic *pīnōną, from Proto-Germanic *pīnō (“pain, torment, torture”), from the noun (see above). Cognate with German peinigen (“to torment, torture”), Icelandic pína (“to torment”).

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To languish; to lose flesh or wear away through distress.

quote.citation: c. 1589–1590 (date written), Christopher Marlo[we], edited by Tho[mas] Heywood, The Famous Tragedy of the Rich Iew of Malta. […], London:  […]  I[ohn] B[eale] for Nicholas Vavasour, […], published 1633, →OCLC, Act I:
quote.text: Why pine not I, and die in this distress?

quote.citation: 1674, John Milton, “Book XI”, in Paradise Lost. […], 2nd edition, London:  […]  S[amuel] Simmons […], →OCLC, pages 299–300:
quote.text: [T]hou mayſt know / What miſerie th' inabſtinence of Eve / Shall bring on men. Immediately a place / Before his eyes appeard, ſad, noyſom, dark, / A Lazar-houſe it ſeemd, wherein were laid / Numbers all diſeas'd,  […]  /  […]  / Dæmoniac Phrenzie, moaping Melancholie / And Moon-ſtruck madneſs, pining Atrophie, / Maraſmus and wide-waſting Peſtilence.

quote.citation: 170?, Thomas Tickell, To a Lady; With a Present of Flowers:
quote.text: This night shall see the gaudy wreath decline, The roses wither and the lilies pine.

quote.citation: 1855, John Sullivan Dwight (translator), “Oh Holy Night”, as printed in 1871, Adolphe-Charles Adam (music), “Cantique de Noël”, G. Schirmer (New York), originally by Placide Cappeau de Roquemaure, 1847
quote.text: Long lay the world in sin and error pining / Till He appear’d and the soul felt its worth

quote.citation: 1994, Walter Dean Myers, The Glory Field‎[1], →ISBN, page 29:
quote.text: The way the story went was that the man's foot healed up all right but that he just pined away.

quote.citation: 2001 May 15, Tool (lyrics and music), “Reflection” (track 11), in Lateralus‎[2]:

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To long, to yearn so much that it causes suffering.

quote.citation: 1969 December 7, Monty Python, “Full Frontal Nudity, Dead Parrot sketch”, in Monty Python's Flying Circus, spoken by shopkeeper and Mr Praline (Michael Palin and John Cleese):
quote.text: Praline: "That parrot is definitely deceased. And when I bought it not half an hour ago you assured me that its lack of movement was due to it being tired and shagged out after a long squawk."Shopkeeper: "It's probably pining for the fiords."Praline: "Pining for the fiords, what kind of talk is that?"

quote.citation: 2016 August 14, Ross Douthat, “A Playboy for President”, in The New York Times‎[3]:
quote.text: Ten years ago, liberals pined for a post-religious right, a different culture war. Be careful what you wish for.

quote.citation: 2019 August 14, A. A. Dowd, “Good Boys Puts a Tween Spin on the R-rated Teen Comedy, to Mostly Funny Effect”, in The A.V. Club‎[4], archived from the original on 4 March 2021:
quote.text: Of the group, Max (Room’s Jacob Tremblay) is the most nominally mature, at least biologically speaking; unlike his childhood companions, he’s entered the early throes of puberty, and spends a lot of his waking hours pining, rather chastely, for a classmate (Millie Davis).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To inflict pain upon; to torment.

quote.citation: 1648, Joseph Hall, “The Breathings of the Devout Soul”, in Josiah Pratt, editor, The Works of the Right Reverend Father in God, Joseph Hall, D.D. […], volume VI (Devotional Works), London:  […]  C[harles] Whittingham, […]; for Williams and Smith, […], published 1808, →OCLC, page 325:
quote.text: Which way, O Lord, which way can I look, and not see some sad examples of misery?  […]  [O]ne is pined in prison; another, tortured on the rack; a third, languisheth under the loss of a dear son, or wife, or husband.
